source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, van Gemund (2006) An evaluation of similarity coefficients for software fault localization (PRDC)
finding: Founding setup. Run a program on many tests. Record which code blocks each run touches (a hit spectrum) and whether the run passed or failed. Rank blocks by how similar their column of hits is to the vector of pass/fail results. Compare four coefficients: Jaccard (Pinpoint), Tarantula's, AMPLE's, and Ochiai (from molecular biology).
numbers: Siemens suite: 7 programs, 132 faulty versions provided, 14 discarded, 118 used. Counts a11 (block hit, run failed), a10 (hit, passed), a01 (not hit, failed), a00 (not hit, passed). Quality qd = rank of the faulty block, ties counted at the worst position.
quote: Ochiai coefficient consistently outperforms those used in Pinpoint (Jaccard), Tarantula, and AMPLE
limits: Single fault only. Failures were detected by comparing output to a correct version, a crude error detector (error accuracy 1.2% for schedule2 up to 21.1% for tot_info). Block level, not statement level.
agent_relevance: S5 on program attempts: the scheme needs many runs with a pass/fail label for each. Our agent has few attempts, so the counts are tiny.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, van Gemund (2006) An evaluation of similarity coefficients for software fault localization (PRDC)
finding: Main result: Ochiai ranks the fault higher than Jaccard, Tarantula and AMPLE on the Siemens programs. Average rank of the fault, Table 2 (Tarantula / Jaccard / Ochiai / AMPLE): one program 10.5 / 7.3 / 1.0 / 2.0, replace 12.2 / 11.6 / 7.6 / 12.7, schedule 3.0 / 2.9 / 1.6 / 11.3, schedule2 31.3 / 31.1 / 25.1 / 34.7, tcas 11.0 / 9.6 / 7.1 / 13.2.
numbers: Ochiai cuts the share of blocks to inspect by about 5% overall; 2.4% to 10% per program versus Jaccard (second best); up to 30% on single faulty versions. Worst case the developer still inspects 40% of the code; best case 1%.
limits: Table text was read from a PDF whose columns are partly scrambled, so row labels for two programs are inferred. The gain is small in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: A small edge in rank, not a different kind of answer. For us the choice of formula matters less than having a usable pass/fail signal.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, van Gemund (2006) An evaluation of similarity coefficients for software fault localization (PRDC)
finding: Why SBFL fails on some faults: the faulty block is run by every pass and every fail (for example main), the fault is deleted code, or other blocks always run together with the faulty block (dependent blocks tie in rank).
numbers: Poor rankings seen for schedule2 and tcas in the Siemens set; ties are scored at the worst rank.
limits: Authors give the causes from inspection, not a measured breakdown here.
agent_relevance: Coverage cannot separate code that always runs together. Same blind spot our agent has when all attempts run the same lines and only values differ.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, van Gemund (2006) An evaluation of similarity coefficients for software fault localization (PRDC)
finding: A mega-LOC industrial check: on Philips TV software all techniques did extremely well, sometimes qd = 1 out of 65K blocks, partly because error detection was ideal there.
numbers: Philips/TRADER case, 65K blocks; reported in the conclusion, not a controlled experiment.
limits: Not a benchmark with many faults; the authors link it to ideal error detection.
agent_relevance: With a perfect oracle the ranking gets far sharper. A trusted check is worth more than a clever formula.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, Golsteijn, van Gemund (2009) A practical evaluation of spectrum-based fault localization (JSS)
finding: Extended study on Siemens plus the space program (162 faulty versions). Ochiai beats the other eight coefficients tested, including Jaccard and Tarantula's. It always does at least as well; average gain about 4% over second best; up to 30% on single faults.
numbers: 162 faulty versions. Observation quality qe (share of runs touching the fault that actually fail) ranges from 1.4% (schedule2) to 20.3% (tot_info) for Siemens, and 50.9% on average for space.
limits: Single-fault benchmarks. Controlled studies are done by selecting runs, not natural test suites.
agent_relevance: Confirms the 2006 result with a second program set. Still the same fault model.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, Golsteijn, van Gemund (2009) A practical evaluation of spectrum-based fault localization (JSS)
finding: Quality of observations: even with very ambiguous failure labels (qe near 1%, only about 1 in 100 fault-touching runs fails) the diagnosis is already useful, qd about 80%, meaning about 20% of code left to inspect. Better labels help, but less than the authors expected.
numbers: qd around 80% at qe = 1% for all three main coefficients; Jaccard approaches Ochiai as qe rises; Ochiai's lead over Tarantula's coefficient is consistent.
limits: qd here is the share of code exonerated, averaged over 162 versions.
agent_relevance: Noisy pass/fail labels still carry signal. A weak check is better than none, but making it perfect gains less than intuition says.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, Golsteijn, van Gemund (2009) A practical evaluation of spectrum-based fault localization (JSS)
finding: Quantity of observations: more failed runs consistently help; the benefit flattens after about 10 failed runs. The number of passed runs has little effect on average, but for single versions it can help or hurt.
numbers: Failed runs NF 1..30 (110 of 162 versions usable) and up to 100 (60 versions); each point averaged over 50 random picks of passed runs; best NF on the order of 10.
limits: Single faults; specific to the benchmark. One program (print_tokens2 v1) got worse with more passed runs, schedule v2 got better.
agent_relevance: About 10 failing attempts is a useful budget. Below that, SBFL has little to count. More passing attempts do not reliably help.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, Golsteijn, van Gemund (2009) A practical evaluation of spectrum-based fault localization (JSS)
finding: Formal result: for blocks hit by at least one failed run, Tarantula, Jaccard and Ochiai each give the same rank order as a simpler expression in a11 and a10 (the two counts that vary by block). Ranking is a trade-off between failures that touch the block (a11) and passes that touch it (a10). Blocks never run by a failed run score 0 for all three.
numbers: Ochiai equals a11 / sqrt((a11+a01)(a11+a10)); Tarantula and Jaccard reduce to monotone functions of a11 and a10 with constants per version.
limits: Algebra done by authors; assumes the single-fault setting.
agent_relevance: The whole scheme is two counts per line. Cheap to run in code, which fits guardrail G5 (code selects, model does not).

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, Golsteijn, van Gemund (2009) A practical evaluation of spectrum-based fault localization (JSS)
finding: Industrial scale: on 150,000 blocks in 1800 files of Philips TV software, SBFL put the fault very high in four real cases, estimated qd 99.96% (NVM corrupt, 96 blocks and 10 files to inspect), above 99.99% (scrolling bug, 5 blocks; invisible pages, 12 blocks), and 99.97% (tuner problem, 2 files).
numbers: Four cases only; authors call the estimates debatable. NVM case estimated indirectly.
limits: Four hand-picked defects, estimated ranks, no control group.
agent_relevance: Scales well when the oracle is strong. Gives no evidence about small attempt sets.

source: Abreu, Zoeteweij, Golsteijn, van Gemund (2006) Automatic fault diagnosis in embedded software (psc06 report)
finding: Short companion paper reporting the same Siemens result (Ochiai about 5% better on average, up to 30%) and its use on embedded TV software.
numbers: Same Siemens figures: 5% average, up to 30%, Ochiai best.
limits: Overlaps heavily with the PRDC and JSS papers; not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Counts as the same evidence, not extra.

source: Jones, Harrold, Stasko (2002) Visualization of test information to assist fault localization (Tarantula, ICSE); Jones & Harrold (2005) Empirical evaluation of the Tarantula technique (ASE)
finding: Tarantula colours each statement by how many failing versus passing tests run it: failing share divided by the sum of failing share and passing share. Abreu et al. say it also has a second brightness value; the coefficient alone is what they studied.
numbers: Not opened. Formula and Siemens use taken from the Abreu papers I opened.
limits: I did not read the Tarantula papers. Their comparison to other methods is not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Origin of the family. A source to open in a later pass.

source: Pearson, Campos, Just, Fraser, Abreu, Ernst, Pang, Keller (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization (ICSE)
finding: Replication of 10 claims comparing SBFL and mutation-based techniques. On 2995 artificial faults, 7 claims held with statistical significance but only 3 had non-negligible effect size. On 310 real Defects4J faults, every earlier result was refuted or statistically and practically insignificant.
numbers: Artificial: 2995 faults from 6 programs. Real: 310 faults. Overall about 70% of earlier pairwise claims confirmed, 30% refuted; 40% of results reversed on real faults.
quote: Techniques that localize artificial faults best do not perform best on real faults
limits: Java programs only, Defects4J. Paired t-tests on EXAM scores; multi-statement faults handled by best, worst and average debugging scenarios.
agent_relevance: The big failed replication for SBFL: results from seeded or mutant faults do not predict which method works on real faults. Do not trust tuning done on seeded bugs alone.

source: Pearson, Campos, Just, Fraser, Abreu, Ernst, Pang, Keller (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization (ICSE)
finding: Ranking flips between fault types. Mean EXAM (lower is better), artificial faults: Metallaxis 0.0432, Op2 0.0503, DStar 0.0510, Ochiai 0.0514, Barinel 0.0562, Tarantula 0.0569, MUSE 0.0781. Real faults: DStar 0.0404, Ochiai 0.0405, Barinel 0.0416, Tarantula 0.0429, Op2 0.0476, Metallaxis 0.0753, MUSE 0.2061.
numbers: Metallaxis is best on artificial faults but near the bottom on real ones; DStar beats Tarantula on artificial faults, no significant difference on real ones.
limits: SBFL formulas end up within about 0.0025 EXAM of each other on real faults.
agent_relevance: Choose a simple SBFL formula; the formula is not where the gain is.

source: Pearson, Campos, Just, Fraser, Abreu, Ernst, Pang, Keller (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization (ICSE)
finding: Practical hit rate on real faults is low. Share of defects with the faulty statement in top-5 / top-10 / top-200: best-case scenario DStar 30% / 39% / 82%, Metallaxis 29% / 39% / 77%, best hybrid 36% / 45% / 85%. Average-case DStar 18% / 26% / 69%. Worst-case DStar 17% / 23% / 57%.
numbers: Real Defects4J faults; the paper cites a practitioner survey where 98% want the fault in the top 10.
limits: The hybrid (MCBFL-hybrid-avg) gain over the best single technique was small in effect size.
agent_relevance: Even the best classical ranking puts the fault in the top 5 under about a third of the time. Treat SBFL as a hint that narrows the search, not an answer.

source: Pearson, Campos, Just, Fraser, Abreu, Ernst, Pang, Keller (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization (ICSE)
finding: Boundary conditions of coverage ranking on real code: 76% of real bug fixes span several statements; about 30% of fixes only add missing code (omission), where no line is wrong; 4% of faults involve non-executable lines and 3% only non-executable lines; 10% involve executable lines that cannot be mutated.
numbers: Counts quoted from other studies of Defects4J and used to define the debugging scenarios.
limits: Quoted by the authors from other work.
agent_relevance: SBFL cannot rank code that is absent. Missing-code bugs (forgotten case, missing branch) fall outside it.

source: Zou, Liang, Xiong, Ernst, Zhang (2019) An empirical study of fault localization families and their combinations (TSE)
finding: On real Defects4J faults, SBFL is the best standalone family (versus mutation, slicing, stack-trace, predicate switching, IR, history). Ochiai and DStar are the best two and nearly identical. A learned combination of families (learning to rank) beats every single technique, with 200% more faults at Top-1.
numbers: Ochiai and DStar locate 156 and 155 faults, about 44% of all faults, in the top 10; Top-1 only 16 and 17 (4% to 5%); Ochiai-DStar correlation r2 = 0.753. EXAM about 0.033.
quote: SBFL is the most effective standalone fault localization family
limits: SBFL is weak at Top-1 because a basic block shares one score across its statements. Learning to rank needs training faults.
agent_relevance: Single formulas are close to a ceiling. Combining signals is where the gain is, which matches combining SBFL with model reading of code.

source: Rezaalipour & Furia (2024) An empirical study of fault localization in Python programs (EMSE)
finding: Replication of Zou et al. on Python: 135 faults, 13 projects (BugsInPy), seven techniques in four families. SBFL is again the best family and MBFL is second, so the Java ordering mostly carries over. Tarantula, Ochiai and DStar give almost the same rankings (correlation 0.94 to 0.99).
numbers: 135 real faults, 13 projects, 7 techniques. Tarantula/Ochiai/DStar rankings correlate 0.94 to 0.99.
limits: Widyasari et al. found Ochiai localizes a lower share of bugs in the top 5 for Python than Pearson et al. found for Java. Tie handling differs between studies.
agent_relevance: Python code behaves like Java for SBFL. Python attempts are the natural domain for our agent.

source: Wong, Gao, Li, Abreu, Wotawa (2016) A survey on software fault localization (TSE); Naish, Lee, Ramamohanarao (2011) A model for spectra-based software diagnosis (TOSEM); Xie, Chen, Zou, Xu (2013) A theoretical analysis of risk evaluation formulas (TOSEM)
finding: Theory line I did not open. The papers I read cite Naish et al. and Xie et al. for results that some formulas (for example Op2) are optimal under a single-fault model, and that many proposed formulas are rank-equivalent.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: From the Pearson and Zou papers I read: single-fault optimality did not show up as a practical gain on real faults (Op2 is fifth of seven in Pearson's real-fault EXAM table).
agent_relevance: Open these in a later pass; the practical result is that formula choice is a minor lever.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization, AutoFL (FSE)
finding: AutoFL gives an LLM function-call tools to read the repository and uses the failing test coverage as input; no SBFL formula. Against Ochiai it improves method-level acc@1 by 19.7% on Defects4J and by 166.7% (GPT-3.5) or 233.3% (GPT-4) on BugsInPy.
numbers: 798 real bugs: Defects4J v1.0 353 bugs, rest BugsInPy. Run time 87.24 s per bug with 5 runs versus 112 s for SBFL as reported by Zou et al.; GPT-3.5 at acc@3 and acc@5 lags SBFL; GPT-4 beats all baselines up to acc@5.
limits: Data contamination possible for Defects4J. The Python gain is larger partly because Ochiai does worse there.
agent_relevance: The LLM beats SBFL at top-1 but not always at top-5. A hybrid that keeps the SBFL list as a fallback fits.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL
finding: Explanation quality: single LLM explanations are accurate about one time in five, but the best of five is often fine. Of 300 explanations, 20.0% described the root cause accurately; for 56.7% of 60 bugs at least one explanation was accurate.
numbers: 300 individual explanations (60 bugs, 5 each). Confidence under 0.25: 23.8% accurate; confidence 0.50 to 0.75: 34.3%.
limits: Hand-scored by the authors; small sample (60 bugs).
agent_relevance: Model explanations need a code check. Repeated sampling gives some chance of a good one, which a code selector must find.

source: Widyasari, Ang, Nguyen, Sharma, Lo (2024) FuseFL: Demystifying faulty code with LLM, step-by-step reasoning for explainable fault localization
finding: Feed ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) the SBFL (Ochiai) ranking, the test results, and a code description. On student programs this finds many more faults at Top-1 than any SBFL formula alone.
numbers: 324 faulty programs from Refactory, 600 faulty lines (1.85 per program). Top-1 faults: Tarantula 89, Ochiai 117, Op2 115, Barinel 89, DStar 115, XAI4FL 149, FuseFL 197 (+68.4% over Ochiai, +32.3% over XAI4FL). 99% of the faults Ochiai finds at Top-1 are also found by FuseFL.
limits: Small programs, GPT-3.5 only, best-case score (any faulty line found).
agent_relevance: Direct support for putting the SBFL ranking into the model's context rather than replacing it.

source: Yang, Le Goues, Martins, Hellendoorn (2024) Large language models for test-free fault localization, LLMAO (ICSE)
finding: LLMAO fine-tunes a code LLM (CodeGen 350M, 6B, 16B) with small adapter layers to rank buggy lines with no test coverage. It beats Ochiai by a large margin at line level.
limits: Line-level Ochiai is weak here because of ties. Fine-tuned on Defects4J-like data, so leakage risk; a trained model, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: SBFL at statement level has ties; a model prior can break them. Ties are the weak point.

source: Qin, Wang, Lou et al. (2025) AgentFL: Scaling LLM-based fault localization to project-level context
finding: A multi-agent ChatGPT pipeline (comprehension, navigation, confirmation) beats baselines that first shrink the search space with Ochiai.
numbers: Defects4J v1.2.0, 395 bugs: AgentFL 157 bugs in Top-1, 28 more than LLMAO on top of Ochiai and 36 more than ChatGPT on top of Ochiai (so about 129 and 121). AgentFL lags LLMAO-with-Ochiai at Top-3 and Top-5.
limits: Baseline counts are derived from the stated differences. Uses test failure output and coverage.
agent_relevance: Prefiltering with Ochiai gives a decent floor; the agent adds Top-1 precision.

source: Xu, Liu, Ren, Zhang, Liang, Lo (2025) FlexFL: Flexible and effective fault localization with open-source LLMs
finding: Two stages: shrink the search space with a classical technique (Ochiai, bug-report IR, or hybrid), then let an LLM agent re-rank. Using Ochiai as the first stage nearly doubles Top-1 over Ochiai alone.
numbers: Defects4J v2.0.0, 835 bugs: Ochiai Top-1/3/5 = 167 / 316 / 389; Ochiai + LLM re-ranker 303 / 421 / 475; FlexFL 350 / 478 / 529 (363 / 511 / 558 with repetition). Without the buggy program text (no code tool) Top-5 falls to 75. Llama3-8B version beats AutoFL and AgentFL (GPT-3.5) by 42 and 63 bugs.
limits: Authors flag possible data contamination and test partly on data the model had not seen. Needs trigger tests and bug reports.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for an S5-style loop: classical spectrum list, then model re-rank. SBFL's job is pruning, not the final call.

source: Rafi, Kim, Chen, Wang (2025) LLM4FL: A multi-agent approach to fault localization via graph-based retrieval and reflexion
finding: Agent system with gpt-4o-mini. The order in which methods are fed to the LLM matters: sorting by Ochiai before chunking is the default, and Top-1 varies by up to 22% across the orders tested.
numbers: Defects4J v2.0.0, 675 faults: Ochiai Top-1/3/5/10 = 121 / 260 / 340 / 413; DeepFL 257; Grace 298; DepGraph 359; AutoFL 275; AgentFL 311; LLM4FL 326 / 425 / 474 / 496. Ablations: no code navigation -16.5% Top-1; no division -23.2%; no reflexion -11.3% (reflexion adds 6% to 11% without external feedback).
limits: One model, temperature 0. DepGraph (a trained GNN) still beats it at Top-1.
agent_relevance: An Ochiai ordering of candidates is a cheap prior that changes what the LLM finds; it can be computed in code.

source: Zhang, Ruan, Fan, Roychoudhury (2024) AutoCodeRover: Autonomous program improvement (ISSTA)
finding: Adding SBFL (top-5 suspicious methods from tests) to an LLM repair agent raises solved SWE-bench Lite tasks; tests are also used to validate patches (3-retry loop).
numbers: SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks): without SBFL 57 solved (19%); with SBFL 66 (22%); 7 tasks solved only with SBFL. Cost about $0.43 to $0.47 per task; time 195 s to 250 s. Of 78 plausible patches in the base run, 51 were correct (65.4%).
limits: Needs a test suite and depends on its quality; the 66 includes patch validation by tests, so the gain is not SBFL alone.
agent_relevance: A small real gain (3 points) from SBFL hints, mixed with test validation. Mind the confound.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: Agentless describes SBFL as the dynamic family but localises with the LLM and picks patches with model-written reproduction tests plus regression tests, not coverage ranking.
numbers: No SBFL measurement.
limits: I read and searched it for SBFL use; it is a design choice, not an experiment on SBFL.
agent_relevance: Shows a way to get the failing run when none exists: write the test. Without a failing run, SBFL has no data.

source: Yang, Zhu, Zhang, Gupta, Kundu (2026) SemLoc: Structured grounding of free-form LLM reasoning for fault localization
finding: SBFL cannot see faults where passing and failing tests run the same lines and only values differ. SemLoc has the LLM write checkable constraints, counts which tests violate each, and ranks by the Ochiai coefficient over this violation spectrum.
numbers: 809 real bugs from 750 GitHub projects (SemBugs) plus QuixBugs. SBFL fails to rank the faulty line first in 83.8% of the 809. In the 185 programs (22.9%) where the faulty line ties with at least half of covered lines, violations alone rank it first in 40.9% versus 2.2% for Ochiai and 7.0% for Daikon invariants. 99.4% of constraints compile to runtime checks; 68.4% of top answers carry a test-confirmed patch and 93.6% of these are correct.
quote: SBFL fails to rank the faulty line first in 83.8%
limits: Authors' own dataset. First-rank accuracy is not significantly different from a plain LLM given the same inputs (81.4% vs 82.0%); a function-only LLM gets 50.0%.
agent_relevance: A modern use of the Abreu counting idea: build a spectrum from model-written checks, not coverage, then rank in code. Closest match to our S5 (counts in code, model only proposes).

source: Xu, Liu, Wu, Kang, Chen, Liu (2025) Exploring the potential and limitations of LLMs for novice program fault localization
finding: On small student programs, 13 LLMs are compared to SBFL (Ochiai, DStar, Op2) and MBFL. All six closed-source LLMs beat SBFL and MBFL. Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) are best; non-reasoning GPT-4 needs careful prompts. Accuracy falls with problem difficulty.
numbers: 503 programs per dataset in Codeflaws (C), ConDefects (Java) and BugT (C++, new, to limit leakage). OpenAI o3 Top-1 312 on one dataset (of 503). In the extracted tables, Ochiai, DStar and Op2 rows were identical in some cells (for example 1 / 8 / 15 / 17 / 20), which points to ties on very small programs.
limits: Table extraction was garbled, so which dataset each Ochiai row belongs to is uncertain; I quote only the pattern. SBFL still found some faults the LLMs missed (one dataset: SBFL uniquely 8, LLM uniquely 1).
agent_relevance: On short programs, a model reading the code beats coverage ranking. SBFL still adds some unique hits.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging, AutoSD
finding: AutoSD has the LLM state a hypothesis, run a debugger probe, observe, then conclude, so the repair is tied to real output. Included as the LLM counterpart of SBFL's use of real run data.
numbers: Opened; no SBFL-specific numbers extracted.
limits: No head-to-head SBFL number found in my read.
agent_relevance: Matches guardrail G2 (revise only from real output).
